Insight into the role of intermittent microaeration in enhancing 
lignocellulose-containing anaerobic digestion and humic 
substances formation
Zhen Jin , Qilin Yu , Zhiqiang Zhao , Yaobin Zhang *
Key Laboratory of Industrial Ecology and Environmental Engineering (Dalian University of Technology), Ministry of Education, School of Environmental Science and 
Technology, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian 116024, China
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Corn straw
Anaerobic digestion
Intermittent microaeration
Humic substances
Methane production
Electron shuttle
A B S T R A C T
Anaerobic digestion of lignocellulose-containing organic matter remains challenging due to slow methane pro­
duction and low conversion efficiency. To overcome these problems, intermittent microaeration has been applied 
to improve the performance of anaerobic digestion; however, the mechanisms are still unclear. This study 
investigated the formation of humic substances and their relationship with methane production under various 
volumes of oxygen (R1:0, R2:0.094, R3:0.188, R4:0.375 mL/(g⋅VS⋅day)). The results showed that methane 
production increased by 29.6 % in the R4 group, while the concentration of fulvic acid and humic acid increased 
by 20.4 % and 32.6 %, respectively. The fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) analysis indicated that 
the formation of hydroxyl, quinone, and carboxylic acid groups in the humic substances might be influenced by 
microaeration. Interestingly, the concentration of humic substances was positively correlated with methane 
production, likely due to humic substances serving as electron shuttles to enhance the syntrophic metabolism of 
methanogenesis. Consistently, the electron transfer capacity, including electron accepting capacity (R1: 0.85 vs. 
R4: 1.86 μmol e−/(g⋅VS)) and electron donating capacity (R1: 0.045 vs. R4: 0.067 μmol e−/(g⋅VS)), was also 
enhanced with microaeration. Furthermore, the microbial community analysis revealed that lignocellulose- 
degrading species were enriched in the microaerobic groups. Correspondingly, the relative gene abundance of 
enzymes involved in the cellulose and hemicellulose metabolic pathways was higher in the group with inter­
mittent microaeration. This study offers new perspectives on microaeration in enhancing anaerobic digestion and 
supports its potential for widespread application in sustainable waste-to-energy systems.
1. Introduction
Anaerobic digestion is widely regarded as a sustainable and eco- 
friendly method to convert biodegradable organic matter into renew­
able energy (methane) [1,2]. Straw is one of the main types of agricul­
tural wastes with an annual production of approximately 8.6 billion tons 
in China [3]. However, anaerobic digestion of straw encounters obsta­
cles owing to the primary composition of lignocellulose, which consists 
of 40–50 % cellulose, 20–30 % hemicellulose, and 15–25 % lignin [4]. 
When the lignocellulosic structure of organic matter serves as the pri­
mary carbon source for anaerobic digestion, it is difficult for anaerobes 
to decompose these complex matters, resulting in the slow organic 
conversion and the low methane production [5].
Recently, it was reported that a small quantity of oxygen or air (DO 
0.1–1 mg/L) benefited anaerobic digestion and increased methane 
production [6]. Air or oxygen injected into an anaerobic digestion is 
believed to promote the growth of facultative bacteria that secrete 
extracellular hydrolytic enzymes such as cellulases to decompose cel­
lulose [7]. The facultative bacteria consume oxygen in a certain extent 
to relieve its harm to obligate anaerobic methanogens [6]. Furthermore, 
it has been reported that Methanosarcina and Methanobacterium can 
produce antioxidative enzymes to survive under high DO level [8]. In 
high-solids anaerobic digestion of cow manure, air mixing system (37.5 
(mL/L⋅min)) increased methane production by 13 % [9]. The air-mixed 
full-scale reactor sustained high biogas yields over a year of continuous 
operation [10]. The enhanced anaerobic digestion with microaeration 
was mainly ascribed to the enrichment of hydrolytic and fermentative 
bacteria to increase microbial diversity. However, the underlying

mechanisms remain unclear.
Humic substances, including fulvic acid (FA) and humic acid (HA), 
are generated during anaerobic digestion via microbial decomposition 
and polymerization [11]. During this process, the organic matter is 
gradually broken down and transformed into more stable high- 
molecular-weight compounds. For example, when lignocellulose- 
containing substrates are used as a carbon source, they can provide 
structural precursors (lignin theory) or low-molecular-weight organics 
(polyphenol theory) that contribute to the formation of humic sub­
stances. Humic substances have varying effects on different stages of 
anaerobic digestion [12]. Specifically, it can enhance solubilization, 
acidogenesis, and acetogenesis, while accelerating or inhibiting hydro­
lysis and methanogenesis [13]. These effects may depend on the con­
centration of humic substances. For example, at higher concentrations 
(2–4 g/L), HA might inhibit methane production by negatively affecting 
methanogenesis [14]. In contrast, at lower concentrations (< 1 g/L), HA 
can act as an electron shuttle because of the presence of quinone groups, 
thereby increased methane production by 16–81 % [14,15]. In fact, 
oxygen plays an important role in humic substances formation by mi­
crobial activities during aerobic composting [16]. Similarly, the addi­
tion of trace amounts of oxygen might influence the formation of humic 
substances, thereby affecting methane production. For example, Zhu 
et al. reported that microaeration during the anaerobic digestion of corn 
straw increased soluble HAs concentration [17]. However, further 
studies are still needed to deepen the understanding how microaeration 
affects humic substances formation and methanogenesis.
In this study, corn straw and waste activated sludge (WAS) were co- 
digested with intermittent microaeration at various air volumes. The 
main objectives of this study were to: 1) evaluate the impact of 
microaeration on anaerobic digestion performance, including methane 
production and organic matter removal efficiency; 2) investigate the 
effects of microaeration on humic substances formation – measured by 
HA and FA concentrations, and two dimensional correlation analysis 
fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (2D-cos-FTIR) – as well as on 
humification, assessed by HA/FA ratio and gemination index (GI); 3) 
elucidate the effects of humic substances on microbial electron transfer 
systems via differential pulse voltammetry (DPV), in situ FTIR, cyclic 
voltammetry (CV), and electron donating capacity (EDC)/electron 
accepting capacity (EAC); and 4) explore the possible mechanisms of 
microaeration effects on anaerobic digestion from the aspects of the 
microbial community and metagenomic analysis.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Substrate and inoculum
Corn straw was purchased from a farm (Lianyungang, China), 
chopped, ground into powder, and screened to a particle size of 
approximately 0.15 mm. The waste activated sludge (WAS) was 
collected from the secondary sedimentation tank of a wastewater 
treatment plant in Dalian, China. The inoculum sludge was taken from 
two anaerobic reactors: one from an anaerobic digester treating cow 
manure in Hangzhou, China (Inoculum HZ) and another from an 
anaerobic digester that used WAS and kitchen waste as substrates in 
Dalian, China (Inoculum DL). The primary characteristics of the sub­
strates and inoculum are listed in the Table 1.
2.2. Batch experiment
The batch experiments were conducted in anaerobic reactors with an 
effective volume of 200 mL, and each group had three parallel reactors. 
At the beginning of the experiment, 10 g of corn straw powder, 40 g of 
WAS, 30 mL of Inoculum HZ, and 20 mL of Inoculum DL were mixed in 
each reactor, followed by the addition of Milli-Q water to achieve a total 
volume of 200 mL. The main characteristics of the reactors were as 
follows: total solids (TS) 81.0 g/L, volatile solids (VS) 56.0 g/L, total 
chemical oxygen demand (TCOD) 80.37 g/L, and pH 7.33. All the re­
actors were purged with nitrogen gas for 20 min to create anaerobic 
conditions. During the experiment, different volumes of air - 0, 5, 10, 
and 20 mL (0, 0.094, 0.188, 0.375 mL/(g⋅VS⋅day) O2) were injected into 
each reactor daily and set as groups R1, R2, R3, and R4 (Fig. S1). All 
reactors were placed in a constant temperature room at 37 ◦C and 
shaken at 120 rpm.
2.3. Physicochemical analysis
The TS, VS, and COD were measured according to standard methods 
[18]. The C, N, and O in the corn straw were analyzed using an 
elemental analyzer (Elementar, vario EL cube, China). pH was measured 
using a pH meter (STARTER, 3100, USA). The gas composition (methane 
and carbon dioxide) was evaluated using gas chromatography (Tianmei, 
GC7900, China) with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD). At the end 
of the experiment, sludge samples from the four groups were freeze- 
dried and mixed with KBr for FTIR analysis using a spectrometer 
(ThermoFisher, 6700, USA). The 2D-cos-FTIR data was performed using 
the 2D Shige software. Data processing was conducted using Origin 
2018, while t-test for data significance was conducted using the SPSS 31. 
The GI was evaluated based on a previous study [19].
Humic substances were extracted from sludge samples using a 
modified method [20,21] as follows: 1 g of freeze-dried samples was 
mixed with Milli-Q water at a 1:10 (m/v) ratio, and the pH was adjusted 
to 1.0 using 6 M HCl. The mixture was shaken at 40 ◦C for 1 h, centri­
fuged at 10000 rpm for 25 min, and the supernatant was filtered through 
Whatman GF/C glass-fiber filters to obtain extraction FA1. The precip­
itate was then adjusted to pH 12.0 with 0.1 M NaOH/Na4P2O7 and 
shaken under N2 conditions for 4 h. The mixture was centrifuged at 
10,000 rpm for 25 min, and the supernatant was filtered through 
Whatman GF/C glass fiber filters. The filtrate was acidified to pH 1.0 
with 6 M HCl to form a suspension. This suspension was centrifuged at 
10,000 rpm for 15 min. The supernatant obtained was designated as 
extracted FA2, while the precipitate was collected as extracted HA. The 
extracted HA was dissolved in 0.1 M KCl, and additional solid KCl was 
added to adjust the K+ concentration to 0.3 M. The solution was then 
centrifuged at 8000 rpm, and 6 M HCl was added to the supernatant to 
induce reprecipitation. The precipitate was collected by centrifugation, 
the supernatant was discarded, and the precipitate was resuspended in a 
mixture of 0.1 M HCl and 0.3 M HF. The suspension was shaken over­
night, transferred to a dialysis bag, dialyzed against Milli-Q water, and 
then freeze-dried. In addition, FA1 and FA2 were purified via XAD-8 
resin adsorption and then freeze-dried. The total FA concentration was 
calculated as the sum of the FA1 and FA2.
2.4. Electrochemical analysis
Both CV and DPV were measured using a three-electrode microbial 
electrochemical system connected to an electrochemical workstation 
(Chenhua, CHI650B, China). The working electrode was a glassy carbon 
electrode (1 cm × 1 cm), the counter electrode was a platinum sheet 
electrode (1 cm × 1 cm), and the reference electrode was an Ag/AgCl 
electrode. 1 × PBS solution was used as the electrolyte, and the head­
space of the electrochemical system was purged with nitrogen. For CV 
analysis, the potential range was set from-0.8 to 0.8 V, with scan rates of 
50 mV/s. The EAC and EDC were analyzed as described in a previous

Electrochemical in situ FTIR was detected as reported by Yu et al. 
[23]. A thin-layer configuration equipped with a CaF2 window was 
positioned vertically outside the infrared spectroscopy chamber. The 
working, counter, and reference electrodes were platinum, platinum 
sheet, and Ag/AgCl electrodes, respectively. 1 × PBS solution was used 
as the electrolyte. The various potentials of the working electrode were 
controlled by a workstation (Corrtest, CS1008, China) in the range of 
−0.9, −0.8, −0.6, −0.4, −0.2, 0, 0.2, and 0.4 V, respectively. The FTIR 
spectra were obtained from 400 to 4000 cm−1 at the different potentials.
2.5. Microbial community and metagenomic analysis
At the end of the experiment, 2 mL of samples from each group were 
taken for DNA extraction using the E.Z.N.A™ Mag-Bind Soil DNA Kit. 
After DNA concentration measurements and quality control, PCR 
amplification was performed. For bacteria, the V3-V4 region was 
amplified using the primers 340F and 805R. For archaea, nested PCR 
targeting the V3-V4 region was processed with two rounds of amplifi­
cation. The primers used in the first round were 340F and 805R, while 
those used in the second round were 349F and 806R. The pooled and 
purified PCR products were sequenced using an Illumina Hiseq2000 
sequencer.
For metagenomic analysis, total DNA was extracted from each 
sample and its quantity and purity were measured before constructing a 
library. Quality-controlled libraries were sequenced using an Illumina 
NovaSeq 6000 high-throughput sequencing platform. Fastp 0.23.2 
software was used for quality control of the sequenced data, followed by 
de novo assembly of clean data using the MEGAHIT software (v1.2.9) 
[24]. N connections were then segmented to obtain N-free scaffolds, 
which were processed using Prodigal 2.6.3 [25] to predict open reading 
frames (ORFs). The predicted ORFs from each sample were combined 
and clustered using the Linclust software to generate a non-redundant 
gene catalog [26]. Finally, the abundance of lignocellulose-degrading 
related gene abundance was analyzed using the KEGG and CAZyme 
databases. The raw 16S rRNA and metagenomic sequencing data were 
deposited in the NCBI BioProject database under SRA accession number 
PRJNA1287080.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Reactor performance
The 40-day batch experiment showed that methane production 
increased with the daily addition of different volumes of oxygen 
(Fig. 1A). There was no significant difference in the accumulative 
methane production among the four reactors during the initial 10 days. 
Afterwards, the accumulative methane production significantly 
increased in the R3 (0.188 mL/(g⋅VS⋅day) O2) and R4 (0.375 mL/ 
(g⋅VS⋅day) O2) groups during the last 30 days (P < 0.05). It might be 
attributed to the longer time required for the hydrolytic acidogenesis 
processes in this co-digestion system, as straw was the main carbon 
source. At the end of the experiment, the accumulative methane pro­
duction in the R2, R3, and R4 groups were 60.2 ± 0.6 mL/(g⋅VS), 67.5 
± 2.8 mL/(g⋅VS), and 77.0 ± 5.4 mL/(g⋅VS), which were 1.3 %, 13.6 %, 
and 29.6 % higher than those of control group, respectively. The addi­
tion of more oxygen has a positive effect on methane production, sug­
gesting that intermittent microaeration could facilitate the hydrolytic 
acidogenesis of lignocellulose, thereby providing more suitable sub­
strates for methanogenesis. Similarly, Zhu et al. also reported that 
anaerobic digestion of straw for methane production was increased 
when the oxygen concentration lower than 0.8 mL/(g⋅VS) [17].
As shown in Fig. 1B, accumulative carbon dioxide production 
exhibited a similar trend to that of methane production, which was also

while it was 11.4 % and 29.3 % higher in the R3 (29.8 ± 0.8 mL/(g⋅VS))

matter was accelerated by intermittent microaeration. Consistently, the 
TS, VS, and TCOD removal efficiencies were also the highest in the R4 
group, reaching 16.5 %, 29.3 %, and 35.3 %, respectively (Fig. 1C).
3.2. Humic substances formation
Humic substances are produced through the transformation of 
lignocellulosic structures by microorganisms [27]. As shown in Fig. 2A, 
peaks at 3400 cm−1 (O–H stretching), 2930 cm−1 (asymmetric C–H 
stretching of CH2 group), 2850 cm−1 (symmetric C–H stretching of CH2 
group), 1650 cm−1 (C––O stretching in quinone), 1450 cm−1 (aliphatic 
C–H deformation) and 1050 cm−1 (C–O stretching in the poly­
saccharides or polysaccharide-like substances) became more obvious in 
the groups with intermittent microaeration [28]. Among them, the peak 
at 3400 cm−1 was related to hydroxyl groups, and the peak at 1650 cm−1 
was associated with the quinone group, both of which were likely 
originated from humic substances, suggesting a possible correlation 
with microaeration and the formation of humic substances.
The 1800–800 cm−1 region of the FTIR spectra was analyzed in 
Fig. 2B and C, as these regions were related to carboxylic acids, carbo­
hydrates, and aliphatic groups [29]. There were five auto-peaks (903, 
1297, 1487, 1624, and 1771 cm−1), indicating the spectral intensities 
detected in the synchronous map. The peak at 903 cm−1 was attributed 
to the aromatic fingerprint region, whereas the peak at 1297 cm−1 was 
associated with C–C stretching in the quinone rings [30,31]. The peaks 
at 1487 cm−1 and 1624 cm−1 correspond to C––C stretching in the ar­
omatic rings and C––O stretching in the quinone rings, respectively [29]. 
Specifically, the most significant changes were observed at 1771 cm−1, 
which were assigned to the carboxylic acid group [32], suggesting that 
intermittent microaeration might influence the formation of carboxylic 
acids in humic substances. Moreover, cross-peaks can reflect the corre­
lation between the intensity changes at two different spectral co­
ordinates. Together with asynchronous maps, the reaction order of 
humic substances functional groups was 1297 > 1487 > 1771 > 1624 
cm−1.
3.3. Quantity and quality of humic substances
FA and HA are the two main components of humic substances [11]. 
At the end of the experiment, the humic substances concentrations were 
measured. The results indicate that the groups with intermittent 
microaeration significantly enhanced the formation of humic substances 
(P < 0.05) (Fig. 3A). FA is a water-soluble compound with a relatively 
simple structure, mainly consisting of short-chain and cyclic compounds 
and serving as a precursor for HA formation. The concentration of FA in 
the four groups was as follows: R1 (34.6 ± 1.2 mg/kg) < R2 (37.9 ± 1.5 
mg/kg) < R3 (40.2 ± 5.2 mg/kg) < R4 (41.7 ± 1.7 mg/kg). HA has a 
relatively complex structure and contains a high proportion of aromatic 
substances. The concentration of HA in the R1 group without microa­
eration was 4.6 mg/kg, whereas in the R2, R3, and R4 groups, it was 
19.0 %, 23.1 %, and 32.6 % higher than that in the R1 group, 
respectively.
On the other hand, the HA/FA ratio is a key indicator of the degree of 
humification, with a higher ratio suggesting a more mature and stable 
transformation of organic matter [33]. The HA/FA ratios in the four 
groups were R1 (0.134) < R3 (0.141) < R2 (0.145) < R4 (0.147) 
(Fig. 3B). In addition, GI is also an indicator of the maturity and quality 
of humic substances, reflecting their phytotoxicity and bioavailability 
[34]. The GI of the R1 group was 62.1 % and that of the R2 group was 
67.7 %, both lower than the national standard of China (>70 %), 
whereas it was 77.2 % in the R3 group and 73.8 % in the R4 group 
(Fig. 3C). Intermittent microaeration improved both humic substances 
formation and methane production. A low concentration of humic 
substances can enhance methane production by promoting direct

3.4. Effects of humic substances on electron transfer capacity
DPV analysis was used to analyze the redox peaks formed during 
electron transfer in the systems. Three oxidation peaks were detected in 
all four groups, with potentials of −0.533 V, −0.335 V, and −
0.046 V 
(vs Ag/AgCl, R4 group) (Fig. 4A). Similarly, three reduction peaks were 
also observed, with potentials of −0.636 V, −0.357 V and −0.164 V (vs 
Ag/AgCl, R4 group) (Fig. 4B). Owing to the complexity of the microbial 
reaction, it was difficult to accurately identify the specific substances 
corresponding to each redox peak. Nevertheless, humic substances also 
contained multiple redox peaks, including peaks at −0.16 V and −0.58 
V, which were similar to peaks observed in this study [35]. Notewor­
thily, as the volume of added oxygen increased, the corresponding redox 
peaks became more obvious and displayed a negative shift compared to 
the control group, indicating an improvement in electron transfer [36].
The redox process of the functional moieties (quinones) of humic 
substances can be characterized by electrochemical in situ FTIR [31]. As 
shown in Fig. 4C, when the electrode potential shifted from −0.9 V to 
0.4 V, several potentials depended upward bands could be detected. The 
upward bands at 1476, 1626 and 1720 cm−1 were assigned to vibration 
of C––C, C––O stretch in the quinone rings and C––O in carboxyl groups 
[31]. These bands might be related to electron transfer and oxidation of 
humic substances in the R1 and R4 groups, whereas the R4 group had 
more obvious band intensities than the R1 group.
The capacitance, which is the integral area of the CV curve, reflects 
the electron transfer ability between microorganisms [37]. As shown in 
Fig. 4D, at a scan rate of 50 mV/s, the capacitances of the four groups 
were as follows: R2 (2.36 mF) < R1 (2.38 mF) < R3 (2.42 mF) < R4

(2.63 mF). A higher capacitance indicates a greater ability to charge or

of the R1 group was 0.85 μmol e−/(g⋅VS), while it increased to 1.41 μmol 
e−/(g⋅VS) in R2 group, 1.48 μmol e−/(g⋅VS) in R3 group, and 1.86 μmol 
e−/(g⋅VS) in R4 group. Similarly, the EDC of the four groups were as 
follows: R1 (0.045 μmol e−/(g⋅VS)) < R2 (0.049 μmol e−/(g⋅VS)) < R3 
(0.058 μmol e−/(g⋅VS)) < R4 (0.067 μmol e−/(g⋅VS)) (Fig. 4F). These 
results indicate that intermittent microaeration with different oxygen 
volumes might improve the microbial electron transfer capacity by 
promoting the production of more humic substances.
3.5. Microbial community analysis
As shown in Fig. 5A, the bacterial community at the genus level 
revealed that the lignocellulose-degrading microorganisms were 
enriched in the groups with microaeration. Specifically, norank_Prolix­
ibacteraceae, norank_Anaerolineaceae, Fastidiosipila, norank_Bacteroidales 
and norank_Christensenellaceae were identified as lignocellulose- 
degrading species. The total relative abundance of these species was 
45.8 % in the R1 group, 47.8 % in the R2 group, 49.6 % in the R3 group, 
and 54.8 % in the R4 group. Among them, norank_Prolixibacteraceae 
(family Prolixibacteraceae), which is associated with lignin degradation 
[38], was the most dominant lignocellulose-degrading genus, with a 
relative abundance of 17.3 % (R1), 25.5 % (R2), 28.4 % (R3), and 21.8 
% (R4). Members of the Prolixibacteraceae family are capable of 
metabolizing a wide range of carbohydrates [39]. Another dominant 
lignocellulose-degrading genus in the four groups was norank_Anaer­
olineaceae (family Anaerolineaceae). Norank_Anaerolineaceae has been 
reported to secrete extracellular cellulase to degrade cellulose and 
enhance hydrolysis, but lacks genes related to carbohydrate-binding 
modules (CBMs) [40]. The highest relative abundance of Nor­
ank_Anaerolineaceae was observed in the R4 group (22.8 %). Further­
more, Fastidiosipila, another lignocellulose-degrading microorganism, 
accounted for 3.6 %, 5.1 %, 5.0 %, and 4.8 % in the R1-R4 groups, 
respectively. Fastidiosipila plays an important role in the conversion of 
complex macromolecular organic matter into VFAs and carbon dioxide 
[41]. In addition, exoelectrogens capable of extracellular electron 
transfer (e.g., Syntrophomonas, Thermomonas) were enriched in the 
groups with microaeration [42,43]. The relative abundance of Syntro­
phomonas was 0.68 %, 1.03 %, 1.25 %, and 0.72 % in the R1-R4 groups, 
respectively.

Generally, Methanosaeta is an acetoclastic species and can obtain elec­

R4 group.
3.6. Metagenomic analysis
Carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) play a crucial role in 
lignocellulose degradation. It can be seen from Fig. 6A, glycoside hy­
drolases (GHs), glycosyltransferases (GTs), and CBMs accounted for the 
highest proportion of CAZymes in R1 and R4 groups. GHs are a class of 
enzymes that catalyze the hydrolysis of glycosidic bonds (covalent 
bonds linking sugar molecules to other molecules) and break down 
complex carbohydrates into smaller sugars or monosaccharides. GHs are 
a class of enzymes that catalyze the hydrolysis of glycosidic bonds (co­
valent bonds between sugar molecules and other molecules), breaking 
down complex carbohydrates into smaller sugars or monosaccharides 
[46]. GTs catalyze the formation of glycosidic bonds between the acti­
vated sugar groups and acceptor molecules [47]. CBMs are non-catalytic 
domains that bind specifically to carbohydrate substrates (e.g., cellulose 
and hemicellulose), positioning the enzyme catalytic domain near the 
substrate to enhance efficiency [48]. The relative abundance of these 
three types of enzymes was slightly higher in the R4 group than in the R1 
group.
Fig. 6B and C further analyze the relative gene abundance of en­
zymes involved in the cellulose and hemicellulose metabolic pathways, 
showing higher levels in the group with intermittent microaeration. For 
example, GH43, including enzymes like β-D-xylosidase, can debranch 
and hydrolyze hemicellulose [48]. The relative abundance was 0.0028 
in the R4 group, which was 7.7 % higher than in the R1 group. In 
addition, the relative gene abundance of CBM3 (0.00029 vs 0.00025), 
CBM6 (0.00112 vs 0.00098), and CBM32 (0.0011 vs 0.0010) were also 
increased in the R4 group. CBM3 is associated with the cellulose enzyme 
catalytic domain of GH, CBM6 is involved in the degradation of cellu­
lose, xylan, and glucan, and CBM32 is distantly related to CBM6 [49,50].

According to the polyphenol–protein theory, some small molecular 
compounds can condense to form humic substances through microbial 
metabolism and enzymatic activity during anaerobic digestion [20]. 
This process can be divided into the intracellular synthesis of poly­
phenolic compounds and extracellular condensation of these poly­
phenolic compounds to form HA and FA [20,52]. The M00004 (PPP 
pathway), M00022 (shikimate pathway), M00024 (phenylalanine 
biosynthesis), and M00025 (tyrosine biosynthesis) modules were asso­
ciated with the formation of intracellular polyphenols and the genera­
tion of humic substances [53,54]. Both M00024 and M00025 belonged 
to the ko00400 (phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan biosynthesis) 
metabolic pathway, and the relative abundance of related genes in the 
R4 group were slightly higher than those in the R1 group (Table S1). 
After the intracellular polyphenolic substances were released into the 
extracellular to condense FA and HA by enzymes such as polyphenol 
oxidase and ubiquinone oxidoreductase [20]. EC1.3.5.1 and EC7.2.1.1 
belonged to the ubiquinone oxidoreductase. The relative gene abun­
dance was 0.00031and 0.00060 in the R4 group, which increased by 3.0 
% and 15.6 %, respectively, compared to the R1 group. This is consistent 
with the FA and HA concentrations (Fig. 3).
3.7. Implication
In this study, intermittent microaeration was applied to promote the 
anaerobic co-digestion of corn straw and waste activated sludge, 
resulting in enhanced methane production and increased formation of 
humic substances. This strategy provides a sustainable solution for the 
efficient utilization of lignocellulose-containing organic waste. Microa­
eration supports the activity of facultative microorganisms involved in 
lignocellulose degradation [7] and influences the structural trans­
formation of lignocellulose, thereby contributing to humic substance 
formation—either via structural precursors (lignin theory) or low- 
molecular-weight organics (polyphenol theory). Consequently, the 
generated humic substances not only enhance organic matter stabiliza­
tion but also facilitate microbial electron transfer, which contributes to 
more efficient methanogenesis. These findings offer practical insights 
for the treatment of a broad range of lignocellulose-containing sub­
strates, including crop residues, cattle manure, and agro-industrial

4. Conclusion
The present study demonstrated that intermittent microaeration 
enhanced both methane production and humic substances formation 
during the anaerobic digestion of lignocellulose-containing substrates. 
FTIR analysis indicated that microaeration might influence the forma­
tion of functional groups such as hydroxyl, quinone, and carboxylic acid 
groups, which are key structural components of the humic substances. In 
addition, the quality of humic substances (such as the HA/FA ratio and 
GI) was also improved under microaerobic conditions, especially at an 
oxygen dosage of 0.375 mL/(g⋅VS⋅day). The formation of humic sub­
stances was positively correlated with accumulative methane produc­
tion. Moreover, the electron transfer capacity was also enhanced in the 
microaerobic groups, since humic substances can act as electron shut­
tles. Furthermore, microbial community and metagenomic analysis 
further revealed that microaeration enriched lignocellulose-degrading 
microorganisms and upregulated genes associated with cellulose and 
hemicellulose degradation.
